newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protesting French truckers tighten grip.
newsitem.headline: Protesting French truckers tighten grip.

text.p: Striking truck drivers tightened their stranglehold on French highways and fuel supplies on Tuesday as unions and employers were locked in a new session of talks seeking to end the nine-day-old dispute.

Union officials said the nationwide protest aimed at securing wage rises, shorter working hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60 for the drivers was growing in strength and putting greater pressure on the economy.

The south and west of the country, including Bordeaux where Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor, were hardest hit. Truckers also sealed off a petrol depot at Grigny which supplies 90 percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the Paris region.
The Oil Industry Association said half the nation's 175 fuel depots were blocked. Heating fuel was getting through but 500 out of 18,000 petrol stations ran dry, up from 100 on Monday.
Local authorities ordered a growing number of petrol stations around the country to supply only fire engines and ambulances, or rationed sales to motorists to half a tank.
Food industry sources said 70 to 80 percent of food supplies had gone through so far and there was no panic buying, but shortages may begin if the protests go into next week.

The strike, the most severe labour unrest in France since a crippling 24-day public sector strike against the centre-right government in late 1995, started affecting mail distribution and disrupting grain supplies to French ports.
The national traffic information centre reported trucks parked across 182 main roads across France on Tuesday afternoon, either blocking or snarling traffic.
In London, British supermarket group J. Sainsbury said it booked two cargo planes to bring in fresh produce from Spain to circumvent the road blocks.
Employers and unions, who have spent the past two nights in talks that have made scant progress on key demands, were locked in a sixth round that began at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Tuesday.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons told the National Assembly the government had offered to help meet some of the drivers' key demands by facilitating early retirement and reducing payroll taxes as an incentive to cut working hours.
"I count upon the spirit of responsibility of all to reach a very rapid settlement to this dispute," he said.
Employers' spokesman Jehan de Marne said they were ready for concessions but wage demands were unacceptable. Truckers want higher wages and pay for hours spent waiting to load and unload.

Government mediator Robert Cros earlier reported "significant progress" with agreement in principle on changes in sick leave, travel expenses and a ban on trucks of all nationalities from French roads on Sundays.
Unions said progress was insufficient to loosen the screw.

The French franc fell because of the protests. Traders said fears the strike could spread, or the government could agree to the strikers' demands, weighed on the currency, pushing it below 3.39 to the German mark.

Force Ouvriere union leader Marc Blondel has threatened to extend the strike to rail and air transport unless a deal is reached by Tuesday. The Communist-led CGT has called for demonstrations and rallies at the roadblocks on Wednesday.

Five rail unions urged members to support the truckers "with the appropriate means". And three rail unions called a 24-hour strike from Tuesday evening at the Sotteville-les-Rouen depot in northwest France, one of the bastions of last year's strikes.
The pro-Socialist CFDT said widening the strike would dilute the truckers' protest.
A two-day strike by pilots, engineers and stewards at Air France and other French airlines on Wednesday and Thursday was set to add to the country's transport misery.

Air France said it would guarantee two-thirds of long-haul flights and a quarter of medium-haul flights. The airline's short-haul unit Air France Europe said it expected to cut more than half its flights.
